item.title: [BBC World] What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
item.description:
Image source, VantorByFrank GardnerSecurity correspondentPublished1 hour ago
Anchored up in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.
The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?
The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.
Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".
It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.
Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.
Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.
The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.
And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.

item.description:
Drone attack on Colombian police base injures civilians and damages homes
Explosive-laden drones have struck a police base in Cúcuta, Colombia, injuring two civilians and damaging 60 homesByASTRID SUÁREZ Associated PressNovember 23, 2026, 12:30 PM
Share
BOGOTA, Colombia -- Explosive-laden drones struck a police base in the Colombian city of Cúcuta Monday, injuring two civilians and damaging 60 homes, authorities said.
Officials did not immediately say who was responsible for the attack on a base belonging to the Norte de Santander Police.
The attack came as President Abelardo de la Espriella steps up military offensives against rebel groups and drug gangs, increasing air strikes and acting on intelligence that has enabled the military to capture several midlevel commanders.
Armed groups have responded by attacking military bases and police stations with small drones, rockets made with gas canisters and roadside bombs. De la Espriella, a conservative who took office in August, has canceled peace negotiations with rebel groups that were underway with his predecessor Gustavo Petro.
Cúcuta, a city of half a million people a short drive from Colombia’s border with Venezuela, is a major trade hub and an important center for criminal groups that profit from the drug trade and other kinds of smuggling.
Rebel groups including the National Liberation Army and the FARC-EMC also operate in the nearby Catatumbo region, where they tax local businesses and promote the cultivation of coca, the raw material for cocaine.
A 2016 peace deal between the Colombian government and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia led to the demobilization of more than 14,000 fighters.

item.title: [BBC World] Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
item.description:
Image source, youtube.com/@ParastooAhmadiiImage caption,
Parastoo Ahmadi's performance was livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024ByDavid Gritten and Ghoncheh Habibiazad, BBC PersianPublished4 hours ago
A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.
Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.
Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.
This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.
In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.
At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.
There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.
On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.
"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.
"The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."

item.title: [ABC News World] EU proposes sweeping new Russia sanctions targeting banks, crypto and sports events
item.description:
EU proposes sweeping new Russia sanctions targeting banks, crypto and sports events
The European Commission has proposed new sanctions against Russia, targeting banks, crypto platforms, and sporting teams competing under the Russian flagByLORNE COOK Associated PressNovember 23, 2026, 12:31 PM
Share
BRUSSELS -- The European Commission on Monday proposed to target dozens of Russia’s banks, crack down on crypto platforms, and slap bans on sporting teams and athletes from competing under the country’s flag in a new round of sanctions over Moscow's war in Ukraine.
The proposals, put forward by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, must be endorsed by all 27 European Union member countries before they can enter into force. The process can take weeks, and the planned measures are likely to be modified.
The sanctions are intended to keep economic pressure on Russia, almost five years into its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The bloc has already hit more than 4,700 people and entities, including President Vladimir Putin, and several energy companies.
Von der Leyen said the move means the EU will be “striking harder at Russia’s way to finance its war by targeting its banks and crypto platforms,” and will be “shutting the door to its participation to European sports and cultural events.”
She said 60 banks will be removed from the Swift messaging system used for international payments. Countries helping Russia to evade sanctions could be caught by the EU's crypto measures, and a crypto sanctions task force would also be launched, von der Leyen said.
The commission wants to target 70 more vessels from Russia’s shadow fleet, which the Kremlin uses to move illicit oil, and to ban all tanker vessels there from European ports. Europeans would be prevented from occupying top posts of Russian companies.

item.description:
WHO director-general visits Cuba as healthcare system breaks down
The World Health Organization's top official is visiting Cuba as the island’s healthcare system crumbles under a spiraling economic crisis and worsening power outagesByCRISTIANA MESQUITA Associated PressNovember 23, 2026, 11:16 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
HAVANA -- The World Health Organization's top official is visiting Cuba as the island’s healthcare system crumbles under a spiraling economic crisis and worsening power outages.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus arrived Sunday at the invitation of health authorities in the Caribbean nation for a three-day visit.
Cuban Public Health Minister Dr. José Ángel Portal Miranda welcomed Tedros, saying it was an opportunity for him to see firsthand the reality of the Cuban healthcare system and the challenges that it faces.
Tedros expressed his willingness to listen and understand Cuba's situation and identify ways to provide support, according to state media newspaper Granma.
“I want to use this visit to better understand the challenges you face and would be happy to mobilize the international community to support you,” he was quoted as saying.
Cuba’s once-vaunted system of free universal healthcare has deteriorated sharply. Analysts say the crisis has been compounded by fuel shortages that they blame on tightened U.S. sanctions on the island’s energy sector, worsening an economy that already had been limping for years.
Hospitals across Cuba face shortages of supplies including syringes, gauze, vaccines and anesthetics. They also lack spare parts to repair equipment such as hemodialysis and CT scan machines.

item.title: [CBS News World] U.S. will host the 2031 Women's World Cup, FIFA announces
item.description:
The United States will host another World Cup, as FIFA confirmed Monday that the country will lead a regional co-hosting of the 2031 Women's World Cup. The co-hosting group includes Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, while a different U.K. project, led by England, was ratified for the 2035 edition. It will be England's first time hosting the games since 1966.
The winning candidates and FIFA president Gianni Infantino promised commercially successful tournaments — the first editions with 48 teams and 104 games — and to reinvest all that money in women's soccer.
"This will be the largest women's sporting event in history," the U.S. Soccer Federation president, Cindy Parlow Cone, told FIFA members in a pre-vote presentation at the governing body's headquarters in Zurich. "Which means we have to deliver."
FIFA wanted these heavyweights of women's soccer to face no opposition without rival bids and so lead hosting the first expanded tournaments. That will bring parity with the men's World Cup, which expanded to 48 teams this year in the U.S., Canada and Mexico.
The 2027 Women's World Cup will have 32 teams in Brazil.
The U.S.-led 2031 project across the CONCACAF regional soccer body bid offers FIFA a choice of stadiums in 20 cities: 14 in the U.S., four in Mexico plus San José in Costa Rica and Kingston, Jamaica.
Atlanta, which hosted men's World Cup games this year, is among the U.S. cities included in the U.S.-Mexico-Costa Rica-Jamaica proposal for 2031, CBS News Atlanta reported. The station cited a report released by FIFA earlier this month, which gave the proposal a score of 4.4 out of 5 and noted that the bid "exceeded the minimum hosting requirements in the FIFA Women's World Cup 2031 technical evaluation."
The U.S. bid also proposed stadiums in Charlotte, Dallas, Denver, Houston, Kansas City, Los Angeles, Minneapolis and Nashville, in addition to MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where the men's final took place in July.

How Ukraine drone attacks on Russian ships unfoldedByHafsa Khalil and Joe Inwood, World news correspondentPublished22 November 2026Updated 6 hours ago
A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones at a port in Libya on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
There was an explosion on the warship at the Benghazi naval base in the early morning, while it was docking for fuel and supplies ahead of its return to Russia, local authorities said.
Zelensky added that Ukraine's attack hit a second Russian vessel, a cargo ship which he claimed was being used to transport weapons.
The local health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast of the port. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.
Following the strikes, the Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.
Libya's two governments - the UN-recognised government in the capital, Tripoli, and a rival administration in the east - have both condemned the attack.
The Tripoli foreign ministry said the country would not accept being drawn into the conflict.
It said foreign forces would not be allowed to use Libyan ports and civilian infrastructure for military purposes.
The eastern government, based in Benghazi, called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty.
Seven naval drones were deployed to target and sink the corvette Merkury, one of Russia's newest ships, Zelensky said in a statement on Monday. He added that a Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed.
The Ukrainian president said the second ship was the MV ANGARA, a Russian container carrier.

item.title: [BBC China] China issues Mount Fuji warning as family of missing climber offers reward
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
The $75,000 reward offered by Chen Jie's family has sparked fears of more reckless climbing attemptsByKelly NgPublished20 November 2026
The Chinese embassy in Japan has warned its citizens against off-season ascents of Mount Fuji amid concerns that the hefty reward offered by a missing hiker's family could encourage more reckless climbing.
Chen Jie, 25, vanished on 8 November on the mountain. His family is offering 500,000 yuan ($75,000; £57,300) to anyone who finds him alive, and 100,000 yuan to anyone who recovers his body, say Chinese and Japanese media reports.
Strong winds and blizzards pose serious risks during the closed season, especially as shelter and first-aid centres are not operational, the embassy said on Tuesday.
Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from around early July to early September.
Earlier this year, authorities of Yamanashi province, where the northern part of Mount Fuji sits, had said that people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service from next year on.
Authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season to submit detailed climbing plans.
"We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Kotaro Nagasaki, the prefecture governor, said at the time.
On Wednesday, Nagasaki told reporters that attempts to find the missing climber could lead to "secondary disasters".
According to Japanese news outlet the Mainichi Shimbun, Nagasaki appeared to appeal to Chen's family, saying: "I understand that your family is important, but please refrain from doing anything that could endanger others."
Some social media users in Japan have similarly expressed fears would entice people to venture into the mountains ill-prepared and lead to more accidents.

item.description:

The visuals of the historic trilateral meeting may be the only lasting impression left by the summitByAnthony ZurcherNorth America correspondentPublished19 November 2026
Donald Trump went into his trilateral meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping with little on the agenda and no clear asks – and he left with little in return.
In the end, the visuals of the meeting – the "optics", as political wags like to say – may be the only lasting impression from the summit, billed by some as a historic "Yalta 2.0" meeting of great powers.
The pomp and the ceremony, in the end, may be what the US president wanted most. Trump, bruised by his Republican Party's drubbing in midterm congressional elections earlier this month, clearly relished the global spotlight during his three-day trip to Asia and the historic nature of the first-ever US-Russia-China trilateral meeting.

That might appear to be a low bar, but it's one that could satisfy the American president.
